knowledge/governance-ladder.title: The governance ladder
knowledge/governance-ladder.body:
Governance here is a ladder, not a gate. Demanding the top rung of a project on
the bottom one is a bug, not rigour.

## Where every record starts

A document needs a title and a status. That is the whole requirement, and a
record of such documents is already publishable, searchable and citable.

## The rungs above it

Each rung is worth climbing when the domain asks for it, and not before.

> [!TIP]
> Climb one rung at a time, and only when something has gone wrong without it.
> A record that adds owners before anyone disputes a document spends review
> effort buying nothing.

### Owners and sources

An owner names who stands behind a document. Provenance names where its claims
came from, one entry per source.

### Effective dates and supersession

An effective date says when a document began to apply. A replaced document is
marked and points at its successor rather than being deleted, so the history
stays readable.

### A measured floor for abstention

The served rung answers questions from the record and declines the ones it does
not cover. The threshold for declining is measured against this corpus, never
copied from another one, and it is recorded beside the number with its date.

knowledge/how-to-write-product-reviews.title: How to Write Amazon Product Reviews That Convert
knowledge/how-to-write-product-reviews.body:
A great Amazon review does more work than the product itself — it's what turns
a curious visitor into someone who trusts your recommendation enough to click
through and buy. The product page can't build that trust; only your review
can. This guide covers how to structure a review, what disclosure rules apply,
how to place affiliate links without pushing readers away, and the SEO basics
that get review pages found in the first place.

## The Review Structure That Converts

- **Hook**: Open with one sentence that shows you understand exactly why the
  reader searched for this — the problem they're trying to solve, not a
  generic product description.
- **Hands-on impression**: Describe how the product actually behaved in use —
  setup, first impressions, anything that surprised you. This is the section
  that separates a real review from a spun-up product listing.
- **Pros and cons**: A short, honest list of both. A review with zero
  downsides reads as an ad, not a review.
- **Who it's for**: Name the specific reader this product suits (and, just as
  important, who should skip it). This is what lets a reader self-select
  instead of guessing.
- **Verdict**: One clear closing judgment — buy it, skip it, or buy the
  alternative you mention. A reader who finishes the review without a clear
  answer won't click through.

## Honesty and Disclosure Rules

Disclosure isn't optional, and it isn't a footer checkbox — it has to be clear
and conspicuous, placed where a reader will actually see it before they act on
the review, not buried at the bottom of the page.[^ftc-endorsement-guides]

- **Disclose near the top**: Place the affiliate disclosure before or
  alongside the first affiliate link, not only in a site-wide footer or
  About page.
- **Use Amazon's required wording**: The Amazon Associates Program requires
  a specific disclosure statement (for example, "As an Amazon Associate I
  earn from qualifying purchases") on every page carrying affiliate
  links.[^amazon-associates-operating-agreement]
- **Never claim hands-on experience you don't have**: If you haven't used the
  product, say so and base the review on verifiable specs, manufacturer
  documentation, and buyer feedback instead of inventing a first-person
  account.
- **Don't hide sponsorship**: If a review unit was provided free or a brand
  paid for the placement, disclose that too — it's a separate obligation from
  the affiliate-link disclosure.

## Placing Affiliate Links Naturally

- **First mention, early**: Link the product once near the top, so a reader
  who's already decided doesn't have to hunt for it.
- **After the pros and cons**: A second link once the reader has the full
  picture and is deciding.
- **Verdict CTA**: A clear final link tied to the verdict — this is usually
  the highest-converting placement on the page.
- **Natural anchor text**: Link the product name or a specific phrase
  ("check current price on Amazon"), never a bare "click here."
- **Don't overlink**: Repeating the same link every paragraph reads as
  spam and depresses click-through rather than raising it.

## What Converts vs. What Kills Trust

| Converts | Kills Trust |
| --- | --- |
| Specific details (measurements, battery life, how it performed on a real task) | Vague praise ("this is amazing", "highly recommend") with no detail |
| Honest, disclosed cons | A review with no downsides at all |
| Real photos or screenshots you took | Stock or manufacturer images only |
| One clear verdict | A hedged, wishy-washy conclusion that doesn't commit |
| Disclosure placed where it's seen | Disclosure buried in a footer or About page |

## SEO Basics for Review Pages

- **Title tag pattern**: Product name + "review" + the current year (e.g.
  "XYZ Blender Review (2026): Is It Worth It?") — this matches how people
  actually search for reviews.
- **Target review-intent keywords**: Phrases like "[product] review,"
  "[product] worth it," and "[product] vs [competitor]" carry buying intent,
  not just informational intent.
- **Add Review structured data**: Schema.org `Review` / `AggregateRating`
  markup lets Google show a star rating directly in search results, which
  raises click-through before the reader even lands on the page.
- **Link related reviews and comparisons internally**: Point to other reviews
  and "X vs Y" pieces on the same or competing products — it keeps readers on
  the site and signals topical depth to search engines.
- **Keep it current**: Update the review when the price, model number, or
  available features change. A stale review is a fast way to lose both
  rankings and reader trust.

knowledge/product-listing.title: Building Product Listings That Convert
knowledge/product-listing.body:
A listing is the compact unit a reader scans before deciding whether to
click at all — it has to do in a few seconds what a full review does in
several paragraphs. A roundup, a comparison table, or a homepage grid lives
or dies on how well its individual listings are built, independent of how
good the surrounding writing is.

## Anatomy of a High-Converting Listing

- **Image**: the product's real Amazon image, sourced properly (see
  `product-sourcing.md`) — never a placeholder or an unrelated stock photo.
- **Title**: the actual product name, not a SKU or an abbreviated internal
  label.
- **Price**: shown with a "price may vary" note. Amazon does not allow a
  static price to be portrayed as guaranteed, since prices change on
  Amazon's own site independently of yours.[^amazon-associates-operating-agreement]
- **Rating and review count**: only if it is genuinely current — a
  fabricated or long-stale rating is worse than showing none at all.
- **A one-line verdict**: who the product is actually for, in one
  sentence.
- **2–3 key-feature bullets**: the specific details a reader needs to tell
  this listing apart from the next one in the same roundup.
- **A naturally-phrased call to action**: "Check Price on Amazon" or "View
  on Amazon," never a bare "click here."

## Listing Formats

- **Table format**: several products compared side by side on the same
  attributes — best when the reader is actively choosing between close
  alternatives.
- **Card grid**: a visual grid of individual listing cards, the common
  shape for a "best of" roundup.
- **Inline numbered list**: each listing as a block inside a longer-form
  article, best when the surrounding prose needs to say something distinct
  about each pick before moving to the next.

## Ordering and Ranking

If a page claims to show the "best" products, the order it lists them in
is itself a claim — say what it's ranked by (value, popularity, a specific
feature) rather than leaving a reader to assume the order is arbitrary or,
worse, paid placement.

## Disclosure on Listings

The same disclosure rule that applies to a full review applies to a
listing block: a page with several listings needs the affiliate
relationship disclosed clearly and conspicuously, not buried once at the
very top of a long page a reader may have scrolled past
already.[^ftc-endorsement-guides]

## What Kills a Listing's Conversion

| Converts | Kills conversion |
| --- | --- |
| Current price, checked recently | Stale price or a dead link |
| The product's real image | A missing or generic placeholder image |
| A specific one-line verdict | A vague "great product!" caption |
| Clear disclosure near the listing | No disclosure anywhere on the page |
| 2–3 concrete feature bullets | No detail beyond the title and price |

knowledge/product-sourcing.title: Sourcing Product Data the Right Way
knowledge/product-sourcing.body:
Picking a good product to promote is only half the job — you then need its
image, price, and details on your own page, kept accurate and licensed
correctly. Getting this step wrong is how affiliates end up with broken
images, stale prices, and the kind of copied content that gets a site
penalized rather than ranked.

## Where Product Data Comes From

- **SiteStripe**: the toolbar Amazon Associates gives approved members
  while they browse Amazon itself — it generates an affiliate link, and
  grabs the product's official image and text, directly from the live
  product page. This is the simplest way to source a single product
  correctly, and it's Amazon's own intended workflow for it.
- **The Product Advertising API (PA-API)**: a programmatic feed of prices,
  images, titles, and availability, meant for sourcing many products at
  once or keeping a large site's listings updated automatically. Access is
  gated — an account needs an approved Associates status and a qualifying
  level of recent sales activity before Amazon grants API access.
- **Manual copy**: opening a product page and copying the price, title, and
  description by hand. The simplest option with no tooling required, and
  also the one most likely to go stale, since nothing reminds you to check
  it again.

## Image and Content Licensing Rules

Only use Amazon's own product images, and only through one of the two
approved methods above — SiteStripe or the PA-API. The Operating Agreement
governs what an Associate may and may not do with Amazon's content, and
pulling images from a third-party site, a competitor's page, or a general
image search is outside that license, whatever the image actually
shows.[^amazon-associates-operating-agreement]

- **Don't hotlink or screenshot from unrelated sites.** An image that
  happens to show the right product but didn't come from Amazon's own
  approved tools isn't licensed for your use, even if it's technically
  accurate.
- **Don't alter product images** beyond simple resizing — adding your own
  text, logos, or edits to an Amazon product photo goes beyond what the
  license covers.

## Keeping Data Fresh

A price or availability status sourced once and never rechecked rots
quietly: the product goes out of stock, the price rises or falls, or the
listing is discontinued, and the page keeps confidently showing the old
information to every visitor.

- **Recheck high-traffic pages more often.** A page bringing in real clicks
  is worth a monthly (or more frequent) spot-check; a low-traffic page can
  go longer between checks.
- **Recheck automatically where you can.** A PA-API-backed page can pull
  current data on every load or on a schedule — this is the main reason
  larger sites invest in API access rather than manual updates.
- **Watch for discontinued products specifically.** A dead product page is
  worse than a slightly stale price — it sends a paying visitor to a dead
  end.

## Red Flags to Avoid

- **Scraping third-party sites for Amazon images or copy** instead of
  using SiteStripe or the PA-API — outside the license, and often lower
  quality besides.
- **Promoting a product whose listing has changed materially** — a
  different variant, a big price jump, or a discontinued status — without
  updating your own page to match.
- **Copying another affiliate's review text or listing copy.** Beyond the
  plagiarism problem, duplicate content is exactly what search engines and
  Amazon itself scrutinize a thin affiliate site for.

knowledge/refund-policy.title: Amazon Returns and Refunds: What Affiliates Need to Know
knowledge/refund-policy.body:
A commission you've already seen appear in your Associates dashboard isn't
necessarily money you'll actually get paid — if the customer returns the
item, Amazon reverses the commission along with the sale. Understanding
when and why that happens matters as much as understanding how you earned
the commission in the first place.

## How Returns Affect Your Commission

A commission is only earned on a **qualifying purchase** — a completed,
kept sale. If a customer returns the product within Amazon's return
window, the sale is unwound, and the commission tied to it is reversed
from your account the same way the sale itself is reversed on Amazon's
side. This is not a penalty against the affiliate — it's the same logic as
any commission being tied to a completed transaction, not merely an
initiated one.[^amazon-associates-operating-agreement]

## The Commission Holding Period

Because returns can happen well after a purchase, Amazon Associates does
not pay out a commission the moment it appears. Commissions are held for a
period — long enough to cover the ordinary return window — before being
finalized and released for payment. This is why a dashboard showing strong
recent earnings doesn't mean that exact figure is what eventually gets
paid: some portion is still provisional until the holding period passes.

## Return Windows

Amazon's standard return window is commonly cited as 30 days from
delivery, but this varies by product category, seller, and season (for
example, holiday-period purchases often get an extended window). Rather
than asserting exact day-counts by category here — a figure Amazon changes
without notice — treat 30 days as the general baseline and verify the
specific category's current window on Amazon's own returns policy page
before relying on an exact number for anything time-sensitive.

## What This Means for Affiliates

- **Don't treat a fresh commission as final money.** Budget and plan
  around the holding period, not around the day a sale first appears.
- **High-return categories carry more volatility.** Electronics, apparel
  (sizing-driven returns), and gift-heavy shopping seasons tend to see
  higher return rates — expect a larger gap between what first appears and
  what's ultimately finalized when you promote heavily in these
  categories.
- **A pattern of returns on a specific product is a signal.** If a product
  you promote is generating unusually frequent returns, that's worth
  treating as a red flag about the product itself, not just a payout
  inconvenience — see `product-hunting-guide.md`'s evaluation criteria.

knowledge/surfaces/for-agents.title: The agent surface
knowledge/surfaces/for-agents.body:
Agents reach the record through MCP — an open standard, so one corpus answers in
any assistant or framework its owner points at it.

## Retrieval that cites

Search and retrieval answer with citations back into the record, so a claim can
be checked against the document that carries it rather than taken on trust.

### Abstention is a feature

"Not in this record" is a correct answer. It is never an error, and never a
licence to fall back on what a model happens to remember.

> [!WARNING]
>
> An agent that fills a gap from its own memory has not used this record — it
> has used it as an opening paragraph. Nothing in the answer says which half
> came from where.

## Files beside the interface

The build publishes the same knowledge as plain files an agent can fetch without
a server: `llms.txt` indexes the record, `llms-full.txt` carries every document
in one file, and each document has a markdown twin at its own address.

knowledge/surfaces/for-people.title: The human surface
knowledge/surfaces/for-people.body:
A static site renders every governed document at a route derived from its path,
with the governance it declares.

## What a page carries

Under each title the page shows the facts the document declares about itself —
who owns it, when it took effect — and lists every source it came from at the
foot, one entry per source, so a citation can point at exactly one of them.

### A status appears only when it is a caveat

A draft or a withdrawn document says so. An approved one shows nothing, because
a reader already assumes a document in the record is current, and a label that
never varies stops being read.

#### A withdrawn document names its successor

Supersession runs both ways: the retired document points at what replaced it,
and the current one names what it replaced. Nothing is deleted.

## The record without the site

Nothing here is authored in the site. Delete the site and the record is intact —
it is CommonMark in a folder, readable in any editor.

knowledge/surfaces/overview.title: Overview
knowledge/surfaces/overview.body:
The record is written once and published through surfaces that cannot disagree,
because each derives from the same source rather than from a copy of it.

## Why they cannot drift

A surface is generated from the record at build time. Adding one never means
editing the knowledge, and a document changed in one place changes everywhere
the next time the record is published.

## The two audiences

A person reads pages. An agent reads bytes. Both are served from the same
governed markdown, which is what makes them answer alike.

An agent reads bytes. Both are served from the same governed markdown, which is what makes them answer alike.

knowledge/what-is-a-ksor.title: What a Knowledge System of Record is
knowledge/what-is-a-ksor.body:
A traditional system of record establishes what is true about the current state
of a business: the ledger is authoritative for transactions, the HRIS for
employee records. When a spreadsheet disagrees with the ledger, the ledger wins.

A Knowledge System of Record establishes something else — what the organization
knows and how it should operate. Which policies apply, which thresholds are
approved, what a term means here, and what to do when the answer is not known.

## The problem it solves

That knowledge is usually scattered across wikis, decks, PDFs, prompts and
someone's memory, with no authoritative answer to the question an agent has to
ask: which knowledge should I trust?

### Why an assistant cannot answer that question

An assistant answers from everything it has ever read, which is exactly why it
cannot tell you which of its sentences were checked. Businesses have had a
system of record for decades. AI never did.

## What this record settles, and what it does not

It settles which copy governs. Every answer traces to a document here, and that
document names who stands behind it and when it took effect.

It does not settle whether that document is right. Provenance proves who said
what, and when — the judgement of whether a source is any good is a separate
matter, and this record never claims otherwise.
